content: 1. Iguez-Perez MA, Dominguez-Vazquez A, Mendez-Galvan J, et al. This study compared the sensitivity of a diagnostic test for detecting antibodies against Onchocerca volvulus. The test utilized a cocktail of recombinant antigens in an indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and was compared to a rapid-format antibody card test. The findings were published in Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2003. 2. Pischke S, Buttner DW, Liebau E, Fischer P. This research introduced an internal control for detecting Onchocerca volvulus DNA using PCR-ELISA. Additionally, it evaluated the rapid detection of specific PCR products through DNA detection test strips. The study was published in Tropical Medicine & International Health in 2002. 3. Weil GJ, Steel C, Liftis F, et al. A rapid-format antibody card test was developed for the diagnosis of onchocerciasis. This diagnostic tool was evaluated for its effectiveness and published in The Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2000. 4. Vincent JA, Lustigman S, Zhang S, Weil GJ. This study compared newer diagnostic tests for onchocerciasis, focusing on their sensitivity and specificity. The findings were published in Annals of Tropical Medicine and Parasitology in 2000. 5. Toe L, Boatin BA, Adjami A, Back C, Merriweather A, Unnasch TR. The study utilized O-150 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis of skin snips to detect Onchocerca volvulus infection. This method was evaluated for its diagnostic accuracy and published in The Journal of Infectious Diseases in 1998. 6. Fischer P, Rubaale T, Meredith SE, Buttner DW. This research assessed the sensitivity of a PCR-based assay for detecting Onchocerca volvulus DNA in skin biopsies. The results were published in Parasitology Research in 1996. 7. Zimmerman PA, Guderian RH, Aruajo E, et al. A PCR-based diagnostic method for Onchocerca volvulus infection was developed, demonstrating improved detection of patients with onchocerciasis. The study was published in The Journal of Infectious Diseases in 1994. 8. Boateng BA, Toe L, Alley ES, Nagelkerke NJ, Borsboom G, Habbema JD. This study compared three diagnostic methods for detecting Onchocerca volvulus infection in areas with low prevalence. The findings were published in Parasitology in 2002. 9. Rodriguez-Perez MA, Gopal H, Adeleke MA, De Luna-Santillana EJ, Gurrola-Reyes JN, Guo X. The study focused on detecting Onchocerca volvulus in Latin American black flies using pool screening PCR and high-throughput automated DNA isolation for transmission surveillance. The results were published in Parasitology Research in 2013. 10. Gopal H, Hassan HK, Rodriguez-Perez MA, Toe LD, Lustigman S, Unnasch TR. This research utilized oligonucleotide-based magnetic bead capture of Onchocerca volvulus DNA for PCR pool screening of vector black flies. The study was published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2012. 11. Rodriguez-Perez MA, Danis-Lozano R, Rodriguez MH, Unnasch TR, Bradley JE. A comparison was made between a PCR assay and fly dissection for detecting Onchocerca volvulus infection in Simulium ochraceum sensu lato in a hypoendemic community in Mexico. The findings were published in Parasitology in 1999. 12. Yameogo L, Toe L, Hougard JM, Boatin BA, Unnasch TR. This field trial evaluated the use of pool screen PCR to estimate the prevalence of Onchocerca volvulus infection in Simulium damnosum sensu lato in an area with successful vector control. The study was published in The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 1999. 13. Oguttu D, Byamukama E, Katholi CR, et al. This study described the use of serosurveillance to monitor the progress of onchocerciasis elimination in Uganda. The findings were published in The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2014. 14. Lakwot TL, Garms R, Rubaale T, et al. The disappearance of onchocerciasis from the Itwara focus in western Uganda was documented following the elimination of the vector Simulium neavei and 19 years of annual ivermectin treatments. The study was published in Acta Tropica in 2013. 15. Katabarwa MN, Lakwo T, Habomugisha P, et al. The study reported the interruption of Onchocerca volvulus transmission in the Mount Elgon focus of eastern Uganda. The findings were published in The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2011. 16. Richards F, Lakwo T, Habomugisha P, et al. This study explored the prospects for interrupting onchocerciasis transmission in the Mount Elgon focus of eastern Uganda. The findings were published in The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2009. 17. Katabarwa MN, Eyamba A, Nwane P, et al. Despite 17 years of annual ivermectin distribution, onchocerciasis transmission was not interrupted in the North Region of Cameroon. The study was published in The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2011. 18. Diawara L, Traore MO, Badji A, et al. This study provided evidence for the feasibility of onchocerciasis elimination with ivermectin treatment in endemic foci in Africa, based on studies conducted in Mali and Senegal. The findings were published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2009. 19. Higazi TB, Mohamed H, Zarroug I, et al. The interruption of onchocerciasis transmission in the Abu Hamed focus in northern Sudan was documented. The findings were published in The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2012. 20. Richards FO, Sauerbrey M, Flores GZ, et al. This study provided an update on the onchocerciasis elimination program for the Americas (OEPA), highlighting progress in Guatemala and Mexico. The findings were published in The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in 2011. These studies collectively highlight advancements in diagnostic methods, treatment strategies, and elimination efforts for onchocerciasis across various regions.
